reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Promises the reader will learn which licenses permit holding others' money, how safeguarding shapes a ledger, and how a platform stays out of possession

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Summarizes the chapter's claims: the license dictates ledger design, Stripe is a licensed non-bank while Adyen is a bank, and a platform escapes the rules only by never possessing the money

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Names the two failure patterns the chapter targets: becoming a holder of customer funds by accident and not knowing which entity holds the cash behind a balance

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A harmless-looking diagram arrow into the company's own bank account changes the company's legal status, because holding others' money is reserved for licensed firms

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A license is a design input that fixes what the holder's ledger must contain and compare, as the non-bank Stripe and the bank Adyen show

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Places the chapter in the running example: the two days between Mila's payment and the studio's payout, asking who holds the money and by what right

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Lays out the order of the chapter's sections, from the Larkfield proposal to the ways custody fails

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: The Fourteen-Day Buffer ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield's product team proposes collecting payments into its own account and paying studios 14 days later so refunds can be funded from the buffer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: The Fourteen-Day Buffer ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The buffer would put about 43 million euros of other people's money in Larkfield's account, nearly as much as its yearly revenue

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: The Fourteen-Day Buffer ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The compliance lead blocks the proposal because possessing others' money is regulated, which raises what holding would require and whether the buffer can exist without it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Holding Other People's Money Needs a License ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Holding money for others is regulated because in a bankruptcy all creditors claim the one balance unless a rule and a record separate the customers' part

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Holding Other People's Money Needs a License ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A bank may treat money left with it as its own asset and lend it, leaving the customer a claim, in return for heavy capital and liquidity rules

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Holding Other People's Money Needs a License ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: A payment institution may move customers' money but never treat it as its own or as a deposit, and needs far less capital than a bank

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Holding Other People's Money Needs a License ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: An e-money institution may additionally keep a stored balance for the customer, must protect the money behind it, and can passport its license across the EEA

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Holding Other People's Money Needs a License ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: In the US a non-bank is licensed state by state as a money transmitter under capital, bond and investment rules / for bank-only functions it leans on a partner bank, often through a pooled for-benefit-of account

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Holding Other People's Money Needs a License ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces a table comparing the four license types, flagging that equating US permissible investments with safeguarding is the author's own reading

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Safeguarding Works: A Ledger, an Account and a Comparison ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Safeguarding under PSD2 means either keeping users' funds unmixed, in a separate account or safe assets and shielded from creditors, or covering them by insurance

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Safeguarding Works: A Ledger, an Account and a Comparison ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: As a system, safeguarding is a per-user ledger covered by a dedicated bank account, and in a pooled account that ledger alone determines who owns which cash

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Safeguarding Works: A Ledger, an Account and a Comparison ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The next-business-day deadline forces the system to know daily how much it holds for users and where

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Safeguarding Works: A Ledger, an Account and a Comparison ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The UK's FCA rules, in force since May 2026, require a daily comparison of required against held safeguarded funds and make the firm cover any shortfall from its own money

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Safeguarding Works: A Ledger, an Account and a Comparison ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Safeguarding's comparison is ordinary reconciliation made legally mandatory, so the license determines how a non-bank's ledger must sort users' funds from its own

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Safeguarding Works: A Ledger, an Account and a Comparison ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Warns that PSD2 is about to be replaced by PSD3 and a regulation, agreed but not yet adopted, so article numbers will change

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Licensed Non-Bank Documents: Stripe ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe's own legal pages state that its Irish and UK entities are authorised e-money institutions, the Irish one passported across the EEA

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Licensed Non-Bank Documents: Stripe ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe says sellers' funds sit in safeguarding accounts it alone controls, without deposit-guarantee cover in the UK, and it does not name the banks

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Licensed Non-Bank Documents: Stripe ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: In the US Stripe combines state money transmitter licenses, payment facilitation under named acquirers and partner-bank or FBO arrangements for stored balances, while stating it is not a bank

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Licensed Non-Bank Documents: Stripe ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe's ledger enforces the safeguarding boundary in code by separating bank-backed accounts from corporate-funded credits and refusing transfers between them

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Licensed Non-Bank Documents: Stripe ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe's two recent charters, an operating Georgia merchant-acquirer bank and a only preliminarily approved trust bank, do not make it a deposit-taking bank

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Bank Documents: Adyen ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen states it is a single Dutch credit institution operating through UK and US branches, unlike Stripe's one licensed entity per regime

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Bank Documents: Adyen ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen says its banking licenses exist to connect directly to rails and schemes, speed settlement and let it pay interest on deposits

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Bank Documents: Adyen ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen documents deposit-guarantee protection only for its business-account product, leaving the status of balances awaiting payout unstated / Adyen documents paying out before it has received funds, which its annual report's default description does not square with and nothing ties to the license

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Bank Documents: Adyen ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Neither company's public material identifies the banks or accounts where the money actually sits, and all license claims here are the companies' own

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Regional Entities Are Money Boundaries ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Both providers make the regional license structure visible to integrators, Stripe through contracting entities and Adyen through a separate balance platform per region

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Regional Entities Are Money Boundaries ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Because each region is a distinct institution or set of accounts, moving money between regions is a real transfer, though the structure says nothing about data location

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Places a Platform Can Stand ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: In the first position the provider holds sellers' funds and the platform only gives instructions, which keeps it outside payment-services rules under the possession-or-control test

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Places a Platform Can Stand ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: In the second position the platform becomes the licensed holder and takes on all safeguarding duties, at a cost a vendor roughly estimates in hundreds of thousands to millions

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Places a Platform Can Stand ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: In the third position the platform already holds the money and uses the provider only to send it, so the platform needs its own license and keeps the record

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Places a Platform Can Stand ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Holding money only briefly in transit is no defence, since the rule covers all received funds and short duration does not change whose money it is

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Places a Platform Can Stand ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The author's rule is to stay an instructing platform until a need arises that no provider will carry out on instruction, and to cost the licensed route before collecting funds oneself

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces a comparison table whose provider columns repeat cited facts and whose last column is the author's inference

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The question to put to each provider differs: for Stripe which entity and safeguarding arrangement applies per country, for Adyen how balances are treated per region

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: Mila's €120 by License Holder ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Traced by holder, the studio's share of Mila's payment is a balance at the bank Adyen until payout, and Larkfield only records it without ever holding it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: Mila's €120 by License Holder ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: On Stripe the same money would sit in an e-money institution's safeguarding account, so the holder varies by provider and country and Larkfield keeps a map of it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: Mila's €120 by License Holder ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield got its refund buffer by instructing a longer payout schedule and a held amount on the studio's provider balance, never taking possession itself

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: When a non-bank intermediary's record of a pooled account is wrong and it fails, the bank cannot tell who owns the money, as the Synapse-prompted FDIC proposal shows

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A platform cannot see a safeguarding shortfall at its provider, so it should limit exposure by paying out on schedule and knowing the holding entity per region

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Platforms slip into possession through small conveniences, and the test is whether any account in the company's name receives money owed to someone else

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Providers' license structures shift over time, which affects contracts and disclosures rather than code, so license facts should be dated and rechecked yearly

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Lists what is established: non-bank funds must be safeguarded and are not deposits, Stripe is a non-bank and Adyen a bank, and a pooled account's ownership rests on the non-bank's own ledger

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Lists what depends on context: whether a platform should hold a license, and how much to leave in a provider balance given the protection behind it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The author's practice is to check possession at every funds-flow arrow and to record each provider's license per region as a dated fact

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The whole part describes one control, a statement of who owes whom proven against an outside record, and that proof lives at the provider and cannot be read from a balance / Larkfield's losses came from movements with no ledger entry, so every kind of movement needs an entry, a clearing account and a proving report

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Gives eight questions a team should ask about who possesses the money at each step, how the provider holds and protects it, and what can remain an instruction

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Hands off to the next part: having seen the provider's slow internal record, the reader will next see how much of it the fast developer interface reveals

results.draft_locus: Why Holding Other People's Money Needs a License ¶6
results.quote: Side by side, the four differ on one line that matters to an architect.
results.finding: The outline summary of this unit is 'introduces a table ... flagging the author's own reading'; the spec's controlling idea (only the bank may treat the money it holds as its own) is never stated in the prose, which announces 'one line' without naming it (flow reader A, item A3, could not tell which line was meant). The other 49 aligned units match their controlling ideas in spec order.
Why Holding ... ¶5 (p12): one idea, the US arrangement of state licenses plus partner banks; the partner-bank sentences are the second half of the spec's single controlling idea, not a second idea.

What a Bank Documents: Adyen ¶3 (p27): one idea, that what the bank status implies for held balances and for pre-financing is not connected to the license in Adyen's own text; the deposit-guarantee sheet and Sales day payout are two instances of it.
What to Take Away ¶4 (p48): one idea, the part's five subjects as one control, with the €412,000 as its absence and the course of action as its consequence.
Every unit ties to a supporting claim S1-S5 through its section; the context units (PSD3 caution, charters, hand-off) serve the status requirement of AC-3 or the part closing.

The introduction opens on a concrete scenario, states a disputable claim and gives a roadmap; none of the listed patterns.

The conclusion sorts what is established, what depends and the author's position, then closes the part; it does not open with 'in conclusion', end on a rephrased thesis alone or hold body evidence. The €412,000 is the declared part callback, not a new subtopic.

What to Take Away ¶4 states what no section states (five subjects as one control; 'Where is the money' has no answer inside the provider) and why it matters (the proof cannot be inherited by reading a balance, so write the entry, the clearing account and the outside report). The spec's sentence 'The license decides which claims and which proof' is not stated in so many words.
What to Take Away ¶3 returns to the whiteboard arrow and says what it brings in (a license, a safeguarding account, a daily comparison, an audit); ¶4 returns to Larkfield's €412,000.

The cold reader predicted all ten body sections in the spec's order, the kinds of evidence (provider documentation, the worked example, comparisons) and the tone; unpredicted items (statutes, closing sections) are outside the roadmap's promises.

The answer names holding money owed to others as a regulated activity needing a license (payment or e-money institution), a safeguarding account kept apart from own funds with a ledger compared against it and shortfall paid from own funds, and the alternative of leaving funds with a licensed provider and only instructing, so the platform has no possession or control. US money transmitter licenses are not named, which the EU-only probe did not ask for.

The answer gives Adyen N.V. as a credit institution under the Dutch central bank with direct connections to rails and schemes, and Stripe's Irish entity as an e-money institution with funds settled to safeguarding accounts before payout; it names no bank and says the banks are not named.
